chapters.summary: Council Member Morano introduces two bills ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11: one requiring DOH to strengthen outreach about benefits for first responders and survivors with a notification system, and another establishing an annual 9/11 Week of Service.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano on 9/11 first responder outreach and service bills

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Morano, followed by Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Today, I'm proud to introduce two bills as we approach the 25th anniversary of September 11th.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 25 years is a long time, and there are New Yorkers today who know September 11th only as history, but for thousands of first responders, recovery workers, survivors, and their families, it's not history.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're still living with the consequences.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So my first bill requires the health department to strengthen outreach about the programs

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: available to those harmed by the attacks and their aftermath and creates a voluntary email and text notification system for information about benefits, eligibility, and important deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because a benefit only helps someone if they know it exists.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: My second bill establishes an annual 9-11 week of service.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll always remember the nearly 3,000 innocent lives taken from us, but we should also remember what New Yorkers did next.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Firefighters and police officers ran towards danger.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Recovery workers labored for months, and ordinary New Yorkers gave blood.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They brought food, volunteered, and helped complete strangers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At one of the darkest moments in our history, this city showed the very best of itself.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I can think of no better way to mark the 25th anniversary than to take care of those still living.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: with the consequences of that day, and to pass that spirit of service on to the next generation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I hope colleagues from across this body will join me in supporting these bills, and I think it would be particularly meaningful if we could work together to pass them before September 11th, the actual 25th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Never forget, shouldn't just describe how we remember the past, it should guide what we do today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Jeff, best of luck in your next step, and we're going to miss you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I hope whoever sits in that chair next has a stopwatch that doesn't work quite so well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: He loves rules for sure.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanks introduces Reso 594 calling on the MTA to correct an inequity in its resident rebate program, where motorcycle riders do not receive the same lower effective toll that the MTA recognizes for motorcycles under regular toll structure.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanks on MTA motorcycle toll rebate inequity

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanks, followed by Banks, and then Carr.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Today, I'm introducing Reso 594, calling on the MTA to correct the inequity in its resident rebate program.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: The MTA already recognizes motorcycles as a lower toll class than passenger vehicles, yet under the resident rebate program, motorcycle riders do not receive the same lower effective toll that the MTA recognizes

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: for motorcycles under the regular toll structure.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And this is simply as unfair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We are asking the MTA to create a new discount.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We are asking them to apply their existing toll policy consistently.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: A resident rebate should reduce a toll, not erase an existing toll benefit.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So I encourage my colleagues to sign on to this resolution and join me in calling for the MTA to fix this inequity.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Banks introduces Intro 991 requiring DDC to establish a catalog of pre-approved standard designs for small capital structures, streamlining planning, reducing design costs, and accelerating construction timelines for neighborhood infrastructure.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks on small capital projects efficiency bill

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilor Banks, followed by Carr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you to Speaker Menon for your support.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Today I'm proud to introduce Intro 991, legislation that will help New York City deliver small capital projects more efficiently and cost efficiently and with less bureaucracy.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Too often the city spends valuable time and resources designing similar small-scale structures from scratch,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: resulting in unnecessary delays and avoidable costs and lower delivery of services and infrastructure that our communities depend on.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This bill would require the DDC in consultation with

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: DCAS and other relevant agencies to establish and maintain a catalog of pre-approved standard designs for small capital structures by leveraging proven and

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: ready-to-use designs whenever feasible.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The city can streamline planning and procurement, reduce design costs, and accelerate construction timelines while still retaining the flexibility needed to address unique site conditions or project requirements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: At a time when every taxpayer dollar must be spent wisely, we should embrace the practical solutions that make government more effective.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This is a very important issue.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Legislation is about improving efficiency, strengthening accountability, and ensuring that public projects move from concept to completion more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Whether it is in a comfort station or a maintenance facility, storage building, or other neighborhood infrastructure, New Yorkers deserve projects that are delivered on time, on budget, and with minimal administrative delay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This is a common sense reform that will help modernize the city's capital process and minimize the impact of limited public resource.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By reducing redundancies and promoting consistencies across projects, we can deliver needed infrastructure faster, better, and serve community across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to support this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Amendment 991.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carr introduces Intro 997 with Council Member Feliz, creating a pilot program requiring NYPD to provide in-ear electronic hearing protection to officers, citing studies showing 34% of law enforcement officers suffer noise-induced hearing loss.
chapters.title: Council Member Carr on police hearing protection pilot program

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Councilmember Carr, followed by Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You don't have to be in New York City long to know that it's a city alive with noise.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's filled with loud traffic, blaring sirens, deafening music, booming construction, and yelling, chanting people at our public gatherings by our fellow New Yorkers who are never short on opinions.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Hopefully we all have a place to get away and escape all that deafening noise, but our police officers can't.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Many studies, including one recently done by the National Institutes of Health, have found that police officers are particularly at risk of acute or chronic hearing damage.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Another has found that 34% of law enforcement officers suffer noise-induced hearing loss or tinnitus.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: significantly higher rate than other occupations and more than twice the rate of the general public.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That is why the chair of our public safety council member Feliz and I are introducing introduction 997 a bill to create a pilot program that would require the NYPD to provide in-ear electronic hearing protection equipment to our officers

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: which would reduce the decibels of excessively loud noise while also allowing them to hear their surroundings and maintain situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The bill would also require the NYPD to publish a report on the pilot program's effectiveness and whether it should be made permanent and expanded.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In the future, this may be a program that could be rolled out to other first responders as well.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: These devices can not only save thousands of police officers from unnecessary hearing damage and loss, but also save the taxpayers from the medical costs of treating this chronic health problem.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So I urge my colleagues to sign on to our legislation and help us protect the hearing of those brave men and women who protect us all.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 995 requiring NYPD training on laws governing restraints on pregnant or postpartum people in custody, and Intro 996 requiring quarterly reporting on arrests where children were present. She also recognizes her summer interns.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers on pregnant detainee and child arrest bills

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Councilor Brooks-Powers, followed by Gennaro.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to begin by acknowledging four of my outstanding interns who are with us today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They're up in the balcony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Samira Green, Miles Hibbert, Olana Canoe, and Johan Yul Ivanlisa.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for all the work you have done on behalf of the 31st Council District.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, I'm proud to introduce two bills intending to bring dignity to families in some of their most vulnerable moments.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The first bill, Intro 995, would require the NYPD to train all officers on the laws and policies governing the use of physical restraints on people in custody who are pregnant or postpartum,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: including the protections of our state's anti-shackling laws.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In May of this year, a woman gave birth in Brooklyn Criminal Court shortly before midnight while restrained on a low-level charge without adequate medical care, privacy, or dignity.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This law requires the NYPD to report every year on the officers it has trained on the dignity and basic level of care that should be afforded of mothers in those moments.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The second bill, Intro 996, amends a 2019 law to require the NYPD to report publicly each quarter on arrests where a child was present.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The precedent...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The number and ages of the children and whether each child was left in the care of another adult.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When a parent or caregiver is arrested, a child is often there to see it and possibly left without care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Our city collects no data on how often this happens or who these children are, and with this, we can more accurately direct support to these families and the organizations that serve them.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, and I urge my colleagues to join me in advancing these.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And again, I'd like to just ask folks, if you see my interns on the way out, just speak to them and pour into them.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I love seeing when we have our young kids here taking part in civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Council Member Marte reintroduces Intro 1008, prohibiting the city from diminishing healthcare coverage for Medicare-eligible retirees, including forcing them into privatized Medicare plans. He emphasizes the bill preserves collective bargaining rights.
chapters.title: Council Member Marte on municipal retiree healthcare protection bill

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Councilmember Marte, followed by Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Today I'm proud to reintroduce Intro 1008, legislation to protect the health care of New York City municipal retirees.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: For decades, our retirees served this city with the understanding that when they retire, the health care they earn would be there for them.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Yet, after years of uncertainty, they remain vulnerable to future efforts to privatize their care, restrict which doctors they can see, or impose new co-pays and other out-of-pocket costs.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: This bill will make sure that that cannot happen.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It prohibits the city from diminishing health care coverage for Medicare-eligible retirees and their dependents, including by forcing them into

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: privatized Medicare plans with limited provider networks or increasing what they have to pay for care.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I want to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: This legislation does not undermine collective bargaining.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The bill explicitly preserves the right of unions to negotiate terms and conditions for employment, including future retirement benefits for active employees they represent.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: As we work towards the larger goal of universal health care, where nobody access to a doctor depends on their employer, income, or insurance company, we cannot allow health care people already earned to be taken away.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Progress cannot mean moving backwards for our retirees.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The immediate Medicare

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: proposal may be off the table where retirees should not have to spend the rest of their lives worrying whether the health care they depend on will be taken away by the next administration or one after.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The council has a responsibility to provide that certainty.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to join us, sign on to Intro 1008, stand with our retirees, and protect the health care that they earn through decades of service in this city.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: We know it's going to come back.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We know we see Legionnaires is an issue that continues.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I look forward to the council having this hearing and legislating in a way that helps New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Council Member Schulman introduces Intro 1016 requiring DOH to establish a Legionnaires' disease hotline during summer months and outbreaks, staffed with healthcare providers to answer questions and connect callers to medical guidance. She announces a September oversight hearing.
chapters.title: Council Member Schulman on Legionnaires disease hotline bill

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to start by thanking Speaker Menon for her tireless leadership on public health this summer and for the seriousness with which she's approached the Legionnaires'disease outbreak on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: During the outbreak this summer, too many New Yorkers didn't know where to turn to, who to call, what symptoms to watch for, how to get connected to care.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That kind of uncertainty during a public health emergency only adds to people's fear and can slow down our response.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's why I'm introducing Intro 1016 today to require the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to establish

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: and maintain a Legionnaires' disease hotline during the summer months and whenever outbreaks occur.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This hotline will be staffed with health care providers who can answer questions and connect callers to medical guidance, resources, and care.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Public health information should never be hard to find in a moment of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This bill will help ensure that the next time Legionnaires'disease strikes, New Yorkers will know exactly where to turn.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I look forward to chairing the oversight hearing in September and working with my colleagues to advance this legislation and other legislation and improve our city's response to public health emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: The Council passed a major legislative package including the Scoop Act (dog waste management), year-round outdoor dining expansion, permanent Certification of No Harassment program, Staten Island flag codification, Office of Insurance Affordability, and firearm discharge reporting.

Speaker Menin announced an investigation into prediction market platforms for predatory marketing to minors, celebrated a council employee's asylum victory, and condemned the Trump administration's ending of TPS for Haitian immigrants.

Multiple council members introduced new bills during general discussion on Legionnaires' disease response, 9/11 first responder outreach, retiree healthcare protection, police hearing protection, mental health crisis response, and pedicab regulation.
